# Executive summary 

We have always been of the view that the longer the European debt crisis lingers on, the greater the likelihood that the negative sentiment it created would feed through into an ongoing slowdown in real economic activity.  The result has been a wait and see approach to inventory management that has dragged refined demand sharply lower in the final quarter of the year in Europe that has tempered our global growth outlook for this year.  Interestingly, there have been relatively minor changes elsewhere, with key Asian countries of Japan and China in line with our previous expectations, despite some further downgrades for the rest of Asia.  Meanwhile, relatively stable conditions in North America have affirmed our confidence in our estimate of demand growth there.  The net result of these changes has been to lower global demand growth to 3.5% this year, from 4.6% in our previous report, while we have also pushed out the recovery to temper growth in 2012 to 3.7% from 4.8% previously. 

Similarly, the supply side of the market has also disappointed in the second half of the year, with a number of high profile strikes tipping disruptions over our 5% allowance.  We have lowered our estimate of refined production this year to 19.694Mt from 19.95Mt in our Q3 report.  The reduction in both demand and supply for this year has largely netted itself out, with the result that we now expect a deficit this year of -237kt, compared to -217kt in our previous report.  The continued negative economic backdrop and ongoing bearish tone in financial markets which has weighed on sentiment across all asset classes, including commodities, caused copper prices to remain sluggish through the final quarter of the year and as a result has lowered our 2011 prices estimate to $8823/t ($4.00/lb). 

Overall base case mine production capability is forecast to decline by 0.7% p.a. between 2010 and 2025 with output falling from a peak of ~20.4Mt in 2015 to ~14.6Mt in 2025.  For this year, demand for mine production will exceed available base case supply by c.400kt, higher than our Q3 forecast of almost 300kt but within the range of analysis over the course of this year.  We expect this market to turn closer to balance in 2012, but in 2013 the new material from projects under construction will likely tip this balance into surplus. 

Our smelter production forecast for 2011 now stands at 15.4Mt which is

4.3% higher than was the case in 2010.  Copperin-concentrates contributed an estimated 86% (89% in 2009) of overall smelter output last year with the balance derived from scrap and purchased blister.  Average primary smelter capacity utilisation rates should exceed 87% this year, up from 83% in 2010.  Overall, we expect 4.3Mt/a of new smelting capacity to be set up over the forecast period. 

The majority of the revisions made to our smelter production capability forecasts are largely reflected in the changes to our refinery output estimates and these can be seen in the main report.  Taking these into account, base case global copper refined production _capability_ is now expected to reach 19.73Mt/a in 2011 (+3.8%), 22Mt/a in 2012 (+11.5%) and 23.6Mt/a in 2013 (+7.4%).  However, growth is forecast to slow markedly in 2014-2015, and then to decline from 2016 onwards.  As a consequence, overall global capability will increase by only 1.2% p.a. between 2010 and 2025.  In tonnage terms this equates to an increase of ~3.82Mt to 22.8Mt in 2025. 

Despite the bearish tone to economic sentiment which has led us to defer demand growth from 2012, the market is expected to remain in deficit next year as a result of changes on the supply side caused by slower start ups at a number of projects.  This will mark a third year of global deficit and result in metal stocks moving lower to 46 days as a result of the 237kt shortfall in refined production relative to demand in our latest forecast.  We do not, therefore, expect the market to return to balance until 2013, when an upturn in global consumption growth will be outpaced by an even stronger gain in refined production.  Following three years of deficits, the market will remain fundamentally tight in 2013, with metal stock days set to average 49 and as a result, prices will remain well supported.  We now forecast 2012 prices to average $8371/t ($3.80/lb) in 2011$, with prices at their highest in the second quarter, while for 2013 we forecast an average price of $8315/t ($3.77/lb). 

The strong increases in supply that we project from 2013 onwards will begin to bring fundamental pressure to bear on prices from 2014, with a series of annual global surpluses driving metal stock days higher and prices lower.  This will result in a period of weak prices that will last until 2018/2019 as a prolonged period of market surpluses will need to be worked off before cash quotes can begin to move higher.  In constant 2011 dollar terms, prices will hit a nadir of $4850/t ($2.20/lb) in 2017 as stocks reach 77 days. 

Our long-term incentive price has been increased to $2.75/lb in current dollars over the period to 2025 as a result of miners continuing to experience increases in operating and capital costs ahead of general inflation.  This has been derived from our analysis of mine project incentive prices and projected demand for mine production over this period.

We have noted in our monthly publication that activity in the fourth quarter has weakened at the end use and semis production level, although refined demand is being supported by tightness in the scrap market. There has also been some restocking of cathode to take advantage of relatively attractive prices, in addition to increased stock levels resulting from the use of copper for financing purposes. Our short term view is that weakness will certainly spread into the early part of 2012. China has of course already acted to loosen credit conditions, and we expect further moves to follow which will lead to an upturn in output from the second quarter onwards. The very strong growth seen in Q2 of this year might well make growth look less flattering in 2012, however, with better prospects for year-on-year

comparisons in the second half of the year to result in full year consumption up at similar levels to 2011 of c.8%. 

Over the longer term we remain bullish on the outlook for Chinese demand, although high single-digit growth cannot be sustained through the forecast period.  We expect a much more sedate pace of growth on average of around 6.8% through the period 2011 to 2015, with demand slowing further still to 4.8% from 2016 to 2025. 

**Infrastructure to support growth through forecast period** Infrastructure will continue to account for a large part of overall consumption in China over the longer term, even if in percentage terms this diminishes relative to around 40% of total semis demand today.  Despite the massive investment both power generation and transmission over the past decade, there remains a requirement for further investment in both.  In particular, the less developed western regions of China still need major investment to develop local grids.  Meanwhile, the latest five year plan focuses on energy efficiency and green energy.  Building out renewable energy sources such as wind power over this period will help to support demand for copper both in turbines themselves but also in power networks because of the often relatively remote locations of wind farms. 

**Tier 2 and 3 cities to build a head of steam** The construction market will continue to be a further major source of demand growth in China over the forecast period, although here too the rate of growth will slow relative to the past ten years, which has seen consistent double-digit annual expansions.  Over the next two or three years, growth will continue to be supported by the expansion of low cost housing, which we have discussed on these pages previously, despite attempts to cool investment in the sector and to prevent property bubbles from developing.  Significantly, however, most of the appreciation in prices has been in the tier 1 cities, while prices, and construction in general, in tier 2 cities has

This year’s growth in automobile production of c.4% is low compared to the breakneck pace of the past two years, which have seen output double, however, 2012 looks set for a double-digit rebound. Firstly, cars are increasing the number of electrical components as vehicles become more complex, which is increasing the use of copper. SA are expected to endure a slow but steady decline in copper demand throughout our forecast period.  Despite the 3.2% regional growth anticipated for this year, demand has settled into a routine 30% lower than the past peaks of 2006-2007 when the construction sector was operating at full tilt, and buyers continue to show restraint in this time of declining prices.  Consequently, for the USA we see demand slowly drifting through, hollowing out at a rate of just under 2% p.a.. 

**..as construction sector looks weak for the medium term** Despite an expected pick-up in demand for the first four months into next year, we are not optimistic that any demand strength will prevail throughout 2012.  The overhang in residential properties especially will keep the lid on metals demand for the next five years at least, and with construction in general accounting for 40% of US demand, it is difficult to see any growth coming even during the mid-term. 

**But formerly bankrupt players in the USA get new owners…** Given the decline in rod and tube demand from the construction sector since 2008, it is easy to understand why such long-standing companies such as Hussey and Sherburne Metals filed for bankruptcy over the past couple of years.  By contrast, both have found new owners, which would contrarily suggest that there is indeed hope for the US manufacturing sector.  Equally, while there have been rod mill closures over the past five years – mostly necessary, the sector would say, to bring national capacity into line with demand – there have also been investments which will add to capacity once again. 

Peru’s Tecnofil is the new name behind the revitalised 30kt/a mill at Sherburne, which will endeavour to sell its specialised oxygen-free rod into sectors other than construction (which would be overkill from a quality point of view). Equally, IMC-Metals America LLC added an O-F rod line at Shelby, North Carolina mid-year which will be focusing on the electroplating sector – small demand levels when compared to wire for construction purposes, but nevertheless an encouraging sign of stronger anticipated demand.  The real challenge, though, will come from 2013, when newcomer SDI-OmniSource will bring on its own new 198kt/a rod mill in Indiana, and as this rod will be made from scrap and its drawn wire will indeed target the construction sector, we would expect the pressure on some existing rod lines to be too great.  Like most others, we do not see sufficient strength coming in this sector to absorb this new rod capacity.  If SDI’s line performs as hoped at a cost structure that should be somewhat lower than the traditional (and older) lines using primary metal, the likelihood is that one or two of the latter will be forced to give way by mid-decade.  We had thought such a move would come sooner rather than later at Texas-based IUSA, but its Mexican parent found a new owner in the form of New York-based fund KPS Capital Partners in September.  With KPS also buyi

## Europe 

**Euro debt travails bring demand to a halt** The ongoing debt crisis in the eurozone has resulted in demand stalling in the final part of the calendar year.  End users are taking a wait and see attitude towards their purchases, with this trend thus feeding its way up the supply chain to result in weakness in demand for cathode.  Destocking can of course only happen once and even if producer and consumer caution leads to a weak final quarter of 2011, unless the regional economy completely grinds to a halt, then orders will need to resume in the new year.  Indeed, we are hearing anecdotal evidence of fabricators and end users deferring orders into the new year rather than cancelling them and as such, an improvement from Q4 is already in place in some cases.  This pick up is of course premised on eurozone debt problems slowly resolving themselves and there not being a disorderly break-up of the currency bloc. 

**Long term outlook favours east of region** The question for this publication is whether near term events will have a lasting impact on economic output and thus first and end use demand for copper in the region.  Our view is that they will not, although clearly the risks to economic activity are weighed towards the downside.  The way this translates into our European copper demand forecast is of modest growth this year, but a contraction in 2012 before a steady recovery thereafter out to 2015.  From this point on however, we expect a period of stagnation in European consumption growth overall, with the traditional western European economies experiencing a hollowing out, and with this offset by expansion in the eastern countries. 

**Construction growth hits a ceiling** Looking at the key sectors in turn, the construction sector continues to weigh on near term demand prospects, with no growth in overall euro area construction activity expected until 2014.  The European residential sector had previously been performing reasonably well but this segment is retrenching sharply in line with broadly negative economic sentiment, while the commercial building sector continues to stagnate.  In the longer term, from 2015 onwards the construction outlook remains relatively bleak, with little or no growth expected.  The broadly flat to declining population during this period will be tempered somewhat by the greater number of people living alone. Demand for copper from this sector therefore looks muted at best through the forecast period. 

**Electrical sector in slow burn** The outlook for the electrical and electronic products sector looks a little better than that of construction, although here too given that Europe is a relatively deve

loped market, low single-digit growth is the best that can be expected.  Much of this growth will be related to the expansion of renewable energy, with this having the twin benefits of not only directly improving demand as a result of copper use in wind turbines and solar cells but also in related network and grid investment because of the remote locations of renewable projects.

**Aurubis withdraws from solar business** Aurubis has decided to close its solar cell business amid strong competition and declining prices.  CIS Solartechnik, a joint venture with Cordes & Graefe, will close down by the end of this year as the scale of the business is no longer economically viable following fierce competition that has brought down prices and as such, margins.  The massive expansion of the use of solar has resulted in a proliferation of small companies and clearly, consolidation is required in the sector.  However, this is not necessarily bad for demand for copper from the solar sector as fewer but bigger and healthier firms will likely continue to consume significant volumes of copper. 

**Aurubis closing down Swedish plant** Following on from its purchase of Luvata, Aurubis has decided to streamline its rolled copper operations as a result of structural over capacity in the industry.  Following this decision, the Finspang, Sweden, plant will be closed, with production likely to be moved to the Zutphen mill in the Netherlands and possibly Buffalo in the US.  Operations are due to wind down within a couple of years, with the net result being the loss of around 35kt of downstream capacity. 

**Transportation growth to be centred in east** The transportation sector will develop in a similar way to overall demand for copper over the forecast period with most of the growth stemming from the east of the region, while the western markets stagnate.  This is particularly true over the period 2015 to 2025, where there will be no significant growth in automotive production in western Europe but a much more healthy expansion in the east.  The production of automotive components and semis will also follow this trend.  The outlook for the transportation sector overall is reasonably healthy, not simply because of expected production growth but because of expectations that the increasing complexity of vehicles and the increasing share of hybrid and electric vehicles will combine to lift the average copper content of cars. 

**Go east for European demand growth** We have lowered our estimate of full year demand in Europe as a result of sharply slowing economic activity in the eurozone.  Consumption in key countries is slowing sharply and were it not for strong growth in Russia as a result of the reintroduction of a cathode export tax, overall growth would be negative.  The prognosis for 2012 then does not look good either, with an outright contraction expected before a

modest recovery in 2013. **Modest medium term boost to construction** There was a short term boost to copper demand in the immediate aftermath of the March disaster as a result of the construction of temporary homes, however, this now seems to have run its course and construction sector demand is now slowing sharply. This is likely to be a relatively short term phenomenon though and may well result in an increase in sectoral demand from 2013 or 2014 as investment that was deferred has to take place. The sector should also benefit from further development in the renewables sector as Japan is a major producer of solar cells. New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply. A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-base products into finished articles. New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that purchasing and re-using it. Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply. ## Scrapping rates The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration. The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in non-electrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; in all other sectors, about 10 years. The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years. The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to be the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. ## Scrap usage Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product. Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap. This latter process uses oxidation

, fluxing and reduction, with a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 

Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 80-90% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases. 

Low copper prices over the period 1997-2003 led to a reduction in the availability of smelting and refining grade scrap with a corresponding decline in the processing of this material in countries such the USA and in Europe.  The notable exception has been China where there has been an upward trend in the treatment of smelting and refining grade scrap material.  Economic and environmental considerations have also played a major role, with the cost of environmental compliance often leading to plant closures, particularly in the USA.  This is despite the fact that the cost of recovering one tonne of copper from scrap is approximately half that of recovery through the conventional route (concentratesmelting-refining).  Secondary smelters and ingot markers typically consume the lion's share (90%) of No.2 scrap and most of the auto radiators and red brass scrap. 

## Scrap consumption 

Copper produced from scrap (at smelters, refineries and in direct use) amounted to 8.27Mt in 2010, an increase of 14.2% on the prior year and accounting for 34% of copper consumed. Scrap use posted a strong recovery in 2010, after contraction in the previous two years as declining copper prices resulted in a lack of incentive to collect scrap while sluggish industrial production meant limited scrap generation. **Incentive pricing provides the most appropriate estimate of long-term average prices** For industries such as copper that are in structural deficit, that is, with long-term demand significantly in excess of base case production intentions, we are of the opinion that while there are various techniques used by the industry to project long-term copper prices, _incentive pricing_ provides the most appropriate estimate of long-term cycle average prices.  The incentive price analysis examines the price required to provide an investor a given rate of return for each project, and calculates the price required in theory to warrant investment in sufficient cumulative capacity to meet potential demand.  In this context long-term can be considered the cycle average price over the next cycle, i.e. the decade over which a project would expect to see payback. 

**Our project incentive price over the period to 2025 is $2.75/lb** In terms of long-term average prices, these are critically dependant upon the metal demand outlook and on capital and operating costs.  The incentive price methodology starts by estimating the demand for additional mine capacity after allowing for scrap usage and base case mine production changes.  Critically, in a demand growth scenario involving depleting mines, the demand for additional capacity increases with time and care must be exercised in precisely defining the forecast period over which the average price is to be estimated.  Capital costs have remained surprisingly resilient at elevated levels over the period 2009 to 2010 and there is limited evidence of significant declines in input costs.  Based on our latest update in 2011$, an incentive price of around $2.75/lb is reasonable over the period to 2025; an upgrade from our previous estimate as a result of continued upward pressure on capital and operating costs.  The contribution from mining-specific inflation to mine site operating costs averaged +6% p.a. over the period 2004 to 2009 during a period when average annual copper prices trebled.  That said during 2009 we calculate that mining-specific inflation within operating costs actually declined by 4% (we are currently in the throes of analysing the data for last year).  As an indication of how mining-specific cost escalation could affect incentive prices, we calculate that an ongoing 5% p.a. uplift over the next 10 years has the potential to raise long-term constant dollar incentive prices to $3.25/lb.  However, we doubt that a repeat of anything like the level of cost escalation seen between 2004 and 2009 can be sustainable moving forwa

rd. Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - December 2011 Page 30 of 33 Copper Long-term Outlook # Principle uses of copper Copper consumption can be divided into three main product groups which are copper wire rod, copper products and copper alloy products. Copper wire rod, which accounts for an estimated 55% of total Global consumption (i.e. including scrap) and ~70% of primary consumption, is copper’s main first use. With the exception of silver, copper has the highest electrical conductivity of all the metals. This helps to explain why the principal application for copper wire rod is wire and cable. Wire rod is consumed in five main wire and cable markets which include general and industrial cable, utility power cable, telecommunication cable, other insulated wire and winding wire. In general, wire and cable and copper products are consumed in five broad sectors: construction, electric and electronic products, industrial machinery and equipment, transportation equipment and consumer and general products. Of these, construction is the largest sector for consuming copper, accounting for 33% of total copper consumption. The main wire and cable and copper products consumed in the construction industry include building wire, power cable, copper plumbing and air conditioning tube, copper sheet and alloy products. Building wire is the largest of the wire and cable markets, accounting for ~35% of wire rod consumption. Rising intensity of use, in both the mature and developing economies, will be largely responsible for building wire maintaining this position. The number of electrical appliances used at home and at the workplace continues to rise, particularly in the mature economies, thereby leading to an increase in the number of power outlets needed per building. In addition, recent technica

l issues imply that more copper wire and cable will be needed in the future.  One of these issues, electrical energy efficiency involves using less power to perform a given task by using more or heavier copper conductors.  Finally, good power quality, defined as the uninterrupted, undistorted flow of electricity at the correct voltage, is also helping to drive up the demand for building wire due to higher power quality being achieved by installing additional circuits and heavier wires and cables. 

In contrast to the building and industrial cable market, the power utility market is the smallest of all the wire and cable segments.  However, demand growth for power cable will be supported by both the general recovery in utility investment and the fact that copper, the mainstay of power grids worldwide, still has considerable potential to carry energy better and reduce losses than aluminium. 

Copper tube, which accounts for an estimated 13% of global refined copper consumption, is the largest of the copper product markets.  The two main uses are in plumbing and heating systems and in air conditioners and refrigeration (ACR tube).  The steady proliferation of plumbing amenities in and around the home, particularly as many houses built today within the mature economies have more than one bathroom, are largely responsible for copper plumbing tube demand growth.  Elsewhere, improved living standards in the developing economies, leading to higher demand for air conditioners, continues to boost demand for ACR tube.  This is particularly the case in China and India where improved power supply will lead to a surge in the consumption of air conditioners over the coming years.  Meanwhile in the mature economies, the market is being driven by external factors such as environmental issues, regulatory concerns and social demands for comfort. 

Other copper and copper alloy products consumed by the construction sector include copper sheet and strip, rods, bars and sections plus brass products.  Copper sheet is used for roofing, eaves gutters, drain pipes for rainwater and lining for facades, while rods bars and sections, along with brass products, are used for building fixture and fittings.  In hospitals, brass doorknobs and push plates are widely used because it has been proven that they help to reduce cross contamination. 

Electrical and electronic products are copper’s second largest consuming sector, accounting for 33% of total copper demand.  Copper containing electrical and electronic products include telecommunication cable, power cable, transformer windings, semiconductors and motors for heavy appliances. 

Since the early 1990s copper telecommunication cable has been largely substituted by fibre optic cable in long distance networks.  However, owing to its high cost, copper telecom cable has remained the preferred link between the main network and consumers.  In addition, the development of the internet and e-mail has further enhanced the role of coppe

r in telecommunications in recent years.  The need for information to be carried quicker along the telecommunication network has led to the introduction of asymmetrical digital subscriber line technology (ADSL).  The ADSL is a dedicated circuit between a home and the telephone company’s central office that uses normal copper telephone lines.  The addition of an ADSL chip to the existing copper network means that users can download files around 15 times faster than an analogue dial-up connection. 

Dramatic gains in copper consumption to have occurred within the home because of a system known to the telecommunications industry as ‘structured wiring’.  The cable carrying voice, computer and television signals is connected to a central hub in the home.  Individual cables then run independently from here to high-quality connections in rooms throughout the house.  Cables connected to the hub consist of four pairs of twisted wires, capable of carrying more electronic signals with less interference and resistance than the older four-stranded telephone wires. Federal Communication Commission (FCC) has set a minimum standard of category 3 cables for new installations, but most builders, not just in the US but elsewhere within the mature economies, prefer to use Category 5 or 6 cable, which is more copper intensive, because they have more than six times the capacity of Category 3 wire and are therefore more than capable of meeting the needs of today’s high-speed Internet services such as digital service links and cable modems.  High-speed digital service lines now provide computer data transmission 50 to 270 times faster than that of the fastest dial-up modem connected to a telephone line.  More importantly, with the number of homes connected to the Internet and usage continuing to increase strongly, demand for higher quality copper telecommunication wire and cable is expected to surge in the coming years. 

The other main wire and cable segment to supply the electrical sector is winding wire.  Winding wire demand accounts for an estimated 20% of copper wire rod consumption, making it the third largest wire and cable market.  Applications include transformers, generators, stereos, television sets and motors.  Indeed, it is the need to improve electrical efficiency of this last application, particularly in the mature economies, that has generated the most growth in winding wire demand recently.  This is because improved electrical efficiency involves using a larger conductor in order to reduce electrical resistance, as well as ensuring that the proper voltages are delivered when needed.  In addition, the efficiency of electric motors is being improved further by introducing copper into the rotor as opposed to aluminium.  Meanwhile, in the developing economies, demand growth will mainly stem from increased consumption of electrical goods as

disposable incomes rise. 

Copper’s third largest consuming sector, industrial machinery and equipment, accounts for 13% of total consumption. Both copper wire and cable and semi products supply this sector which includes equipment and machinery, industrial valves and fittings, off-highway vehicles and heat exchangers.  Copper wire and copper and copper alloy products are also used in transportation equipment, copper’s fourth largest category.  This includes the automotive, marine and aircraft/aerospace sectors.  It is within the automotive sector that developments of new copper applications have been most concentrated in recent years.  Prior to 1930 copper and brass, having excellent pressure containing and anticorrosion characteristics, were the favoured materials to be used in brake tubing.  However, mass auto production in the 1940s led to the adoption of furnace-brazed steel tubing because it was much lower in cost.  Although this form of tubing is still widely used today, copper has re-gained some of its lost market share through the introduction of a copper-nickel alloy (90% copper/10% nickel) which is more resistant to corrosion from road mud and salt than steel piping.  Likewise, new technology has led to the development of a new brazed copper-brass automotive radiator which has the necessary requirements to recapture some of the market share displaced by aluminium over the past twenty years. 

Meanwhile, 42-volt systems, hybrid vehicles and numerous electrical and electronic applications provide additional growth prospects for the use of copper within the automotive sector Over the years the number of electrical and electronic components installed per unit has been rising steadily, thereby creating the need for growth in the power and signal distribution system (otherwise known as the wiring harness).  Many of the electrical components will have to be redesigned in order to work effectively with the higher-voltage systems which could result in the copper content of some of the electrical components falling, but as more power becomes available, new electrical components will emerge.  Such examples include electronic valve actuation and electric braking, resulting in several kilos of copper, per unit, being added.  Forecasts have shown that over the next ten years, increases per vehicle will outweigh the decreases in copper required per component. 

Copper’s final end-use category is consumer and general products.  Copper consumed in this sector accounts for 8% of total copper consumption.  The three main end-uses are electrical appliances, military ordnance and coinage.  The production of the new Euro coin in recent years has helped to support demand for copper and copper alloy products.
